Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? Edward Albee's 1962 play depicts a brutal evening between two married couples—the intellectual George and his acerbic, alcohol-fueled wife Martha, and their younger guests Nick and Honey. Under the guise of late-night games and intellectual sparring, the play exposes the lies, cruelty, and desperate longing that bind marriages and destroy friendships.

The play won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1963. The 1966 film adaptation with Elizabeth Taylor is equally iconic and earned thirteen Oscar nominations. The play contains shocking profanity for its era and raw sexual language. It was controversial and helped break censorship barriers in American theater. Martha's famous opening line, "What a dump!", sets the tone for her savage, witty contempt for her husband's passivity.

The evening is structured around games: Get the Guests, Humiliate the Host, and Bringing Up Baby. Each one is a weapon in the marital warfare. George and Martha have invented a fantasy child who never existed. Its fictional status becomes a symbol of their emotional void and mutual delusion. Albee uses the title, which references Virginia Woolf and not a person present, as a game itself. The characters are afraid to confront the emptiness they have created.

Albee created his darkest exploration of American marriage and the performance of identity. His dialogue and structure anticipate the absurdist tradition of Beckett and Pinter. A Streetcar Named Desire similarly dissects the rituals and violence within intimate relationships. Death of a Salesman examines the lies couples tell themselves to survive together. And The Glass Menagerie explores family myth-making and psychological fragility.
